glossary.Evidence: Information used to support a claim. Check it rather than treating it as proof on its own.
glossary.Cite: Name the source and where to find the words or information you used.
glossary.Relevant: Related to the exact claim, not just the same topic.
glossary.Develop: Build or change an idea across a text by adding details, examples or limits.
glossary.Inference: A conclusion drawn from clues and reasoning rather than stated directly.
glossary.Objective: Giving a fair, accurate account without adding your own judgment.
glossary.Bias: A leaning that can affect which facts someone selects and how they explain them.
glossary.Quotation: Exact words borrowed from a source and clearly marked as borrowed.

faq: Yes. A text can develop connected ideas, such as how people share work and how they judge results. Use the text to decide how many ideas it develops.
Evidence is information used as support. An opinion is a belief or judgment. A sales rank can support a claim about popularity, but not prove that a book is the best.
It lets others check the words and their context. You still need to explain how that evidence supports your reading.
Find the claim and its support. Ask what context is missing. Judge the specific message; do not assume every writer is hiding facts.
Build a possible idea from the details. Explain how they fit. Be ready to revise it when you read more.
You may use exact words if you mark them as a quote and cite the source. A paraphrase needs a source too. Explain how the words support your point.

glossary.Definition: Words that directly tell what something means. They need not be a full sentence.
glossary.Signal: A word or phrase that can show a link, such as but, or or such as.

memory: D-E-S-A: Dogs Eat Some Apples. The letters stand for Definition, Example, Synonym and Antonym.
Use the first letters to recall four kinds of clue. Then find a real clue in the text.
Look at unbreakable. Find break, un- and -able. Together they mean not able to be broken. Cover or mark each known part.
Use parts that really belong to the word. Do not cut off random letters. Check whether the meaning fits the sentence.

glossary.Detail: A smaller piece of information. It may help explain a larger point.

faq: A paragraph often builds one main point. Some texts develop more than one. Choose a statement that fits the part you are reading.
No. A writer may state it later or leave you to work it out. Check the details before choosing the first line.
The main idea names a key point. A summary also gives the most important details in a short account.
It helps you connect details and understand a text. You will also use other skills, such as working out new words or comparing ideas.
You can disagree. First explain the point fairly. Then use reasons and evidence to show why you disagree.
Yes. Pause, replay or use a transcript if it helps. Think about what the sounds and pictures add too.

glossary.Orbit: The path one object follows around another because of gravity.

faq: The Moon can be above the horizon in daylight and bright enough to see. Phase, place, time and weather matter. A first-quarter Moon is often seen in the afternoon; a third-quarter Moon in the morning.
The far side mostly faces away from Earth, but it gets sunlight too. Night moves around the Moon. Over time, we can see a little around its edges. Far side does not mean always dark.

Near the horizon, moonlight passes through more air. More blue light scatters away, so it can look orange. Its huge look is mainly a visual illusion. Its actual angle in the sky changes little during that short rise.
The phase is much the same at the same time, but its tilt can look different. Right-lit does not always mean waxing. Watch how the lit share changes over several days.
The path of a total eclipse is narrow. A place may wait a long time for one, and the wait varies by place. More people nearby may see a partial eclipse.
Yes. Differences in the Moon’s pull across Earth help cause ocean tides. The Sun affects tides too. That is a separate lesson from phases.

memory: Draw three columns: hundreds, tens, ones. Put the ones on the right. Show 245 with two hundred flats, four ten rods and five ones.
Each block stands for a place value. The columns keep the places lined up.
Line up the places. Check hundreds first, then tens, then ones. Move to the next place only if the digits match.
99 has no hundreds. 100 has one hundred. So 99 is less than 100, even though its tens digit is larger.
Look outside the dialogue. Does I name the voice telling the story? That can show first person. Check the whole passage.
I inside speech does not tell you who the narrator is. A first-person narrator can also use she to talk about someone else.
Think of a light showing part of a room. A narrator may show one person’s thoughts or reveal more than one person’s thoughts.
The light stands for what we are told. A third-person narrator need not know or tell everything.
Maya: puddle, wet socks, Dev laughs, I feel hurt. Dev: puddle, splash, memory of yesterday, I laugh, Maya walks off.
They share an event but have different thoughts and knowledge. Neither chain tells us everything. Maya’s feelings are real even if she does not know why Dev laughed.
faq: The author writes the text. The narrator is the voice telling the story. In fiction they may differ. In a memoir, the author may tell their own story.
It uses you to tell what happens to the person addressed: You open the door. You hear a creak. Some games and choice stories use it.
Yes. A narrator can guess or misunderstand. Maya does not know all of Dev’s thoughts here. That does not mean her hurt feelings are wrong.
Yes. Follow the names and what each voice knows. A new chapter may switch narrators even if it uses the same pronouns.
First person can feel like someone speaking to you. It can show that person’s thoughts closely. But the narrator still chooses what to tell.
No. Some follow one person closely. Others reveal more people’s thoughts. Ask what this particular narrator tells you and what is left out.

scarcity_choice_grade7.reading:
## Everything Has a Cost

You have one free hour. Suppose you can choose just one plan: see friends, work on a project, or rest. You cannot use those same minutes for all three.

**Scarcity** means the resources available cannot meet all the wants for them. Time, money, space and materials can be **scarce**. It depends on what is wanted and what is available at that time and place. A free price does not mean an endless supply.

A **choice** selects among options you can really take. An **alternative** is another such option. A **trade-off** gives up one use or gain to get another. Some choices allow a mix of activities. Our one-hour case rules out a mix to keep the example clear.

An **opportunity** is a chance to do something. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option you give up. If you choose rest and seeing friends ranks second, the cost is the benefit of that visit. Do not add every option you turned down. If a mix of activities is allowed and ranks second, count that whole mix instead.

Consider a made-up town. Its budget can pay for a road or a library, but not both. These are its only two possible plans. If it chooses the road, it gives up the library's benefit. In real life there may be more choices. You must find the next-best one rather than guess.

A **benefit** is an expected gain. Compare future costs and gains, including effects that are hard to price. People may rank the same options differently.

A **sunk** cost is a past cost you cannot get back. Suppose a film ticket cannot be refunded, resold or given away. The money is gone whichever plan you choose now. Spending it is not, by itself, a reason to watch a film you no longer want to see. Think about the time, travel cost and experience still ahead.

If you can get a refund or sell the ticket, that value still matters. Past training time is gone, but the skills may help you now. An old tool may still be useful or have resale value. Do not confuse past spending with what an item can do in the future.

A **marginal** decision asks about one more unit: is one more hour of practice worth what you give up? An **incentive** changes an expected cost or benefit. It may influence people without making them all choose alike.

In our task, four groups want one room from four to five. Rank the uses, explain your criteria, and name the next-best benefit you give up. The sort also uses made-up cases. Judge each resource in the stated setting, not everywhere and for all time.

glossary.Scarcity: Having fewer resources than needed to meet all the wants for them.
glossary.Scarce: Limited compared with what is wanted at a certain time and place.
glossary.Choice: Picking among options you can actually take.
glossary.Opportunity: A chance to do something. The cost of a choice is the value of the next-best option you give up.
glossary.Alternative: Another possible option. It need not be the second-best one.
glossary.Sunk: A past cost that cannot be recovered. Future use or resale value can still matter.
glossary.Marginal: About one more unit, or the extra cost or benefit it brings.
glossary.Incentive: A change in expected cost or benefit that can influence a choice.

faq: A free event may still use time. What would you do with that time instead? Name the next-best option. A zero price does not settle that question.
No. You still give up the value of the other option, even if you like both equally. The cost is not the difference between their values, and it is not the same as regret.
No. Time and space choices have trade-offs too. A price alone cannot tell us which choice is best for a person.
It can be hard to stop after spending time or money. Ask what you can still change. Count future costs, gains and any value you can recover.
No. Scarcity means resources are limited compared with wants. Poverty means lacking resources to meet important needs. Its effects are not the same as every everyday trade-off.
Making more can expand choices, but it uses resources. Ask what else those resources could do. Do not assume each worker or material is already being used on another project.
memory: Name your first choice. Then name the best option you could take instead. What benefit do you give up by not taking it?
A runner-up helps you remember second place. Rank only options you can really take, including a mix if allowed.
Draw a line. Put money you cannot get back on the past side. Put future costs, future gains and resale value on the other side.
The line helps you focus on what can still change. Skills and useful things gained in the past can still help now.

faq: Fractions help us name parts of an amount, such as half an hour or three-fourths of a cup. Whole numbers alone cannot name every amount.
Yes. Both land at the same point: 0.5 = 5/10 = 1/2. Some fractions have decimals that keep repeating. For example, 1/3 = 0.333... .
Yes. 5/4 means five steps of size one-fourth from zero. You pass 1 and reach 1 1/4. It is called an improper fraction.
You may be thinking that 8 is larger than 4. But with the same whole, cutting it into eight equal pieces makes each piece smaller than one of four equal pieces. Draw both on the same line.
There is no biggest one. Pick a fraction below 1. The point halfway from it to 1 is a larger fraction that is still below 1. You can do this again.
Yes. Negative one-half is as far left of zero as one-half is to the right.

glossary.Intercept: Where a graph meets an axis. The y-axis crossing has x = 0.

glossary.Magnet: An object that produces a field and can attract certain materials, such as iron.
glossary.Magnetic: Related to forces and fields produced by moving charges and aligned atomic moments.
